extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and anyone learning correct inductive reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Recognize and diagnose errors in observation and generalization when forming inductive conclusions; the page catalogues classes of fallacies (non-observation, mal-observation, faulty generalization) with examples and corrective guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instances more likely to be remembered than others
rubrics_metrics.description: When the instances on one side of a question are more likely to be remembered and recorded than those on the other; especially if there is a strong motive to preserve memory of the first but not the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid basing generalizations on selectively remembered instances; actively seek and record counter-instances. Examples: continued credit to quacks and fortune-tellers because successes are remembered while failures are forgotten; the proverb 'Fortune favors fools' arises from recalling surprising successes of the unskilled while neglecting routine successes of the skilled. Ensure sampling practices that capture both confirming and disconfirming cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to eliminate chance (Elimination of Chance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to appreciate the number of coincidences that will occur by chance between unconnected events, and thus treating occasional coincidences as evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require sufficient numbers of instances (Elimination of Chance) before attributing causal or remarkable status to coincidences. Example: belief in almanac weather prophecies persists because occasional hits are remembered despite many errors. Design inductive tests to exclude chance explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preconceived opinion causing non-observation
rubrics_metrics.description: A preconceived theory or opinion causes observers to be unmindful of facts contradictory to that theory, sometimes even when the contradictory facts pass before their own eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of theory-driven blindness: deliberately look for facts that would falsify your hypothesis. Historical examples: opponents of Copernicus accepting spurious facts; historians reading same sources but seeing only what confirms their sectarian preconceptions. Routine remedy: perform disconfirmatory tests and encourage dissenting inspection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-observation of material circumstances within observed instances
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances on which a generalization is founded may have been imperfectly observed; some important circumstances correlated with outcomes are overlooked, rendering particulars false or insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate and record all materially relevant circumstances of observed instances (both sensory and contextual). Examples: phlogiston theory ignored gaseous combustion products; reputed cures attributed to charms actually depended on bandaging, rest, regimen, or co-administered medicines. Use controlled observation and account for confounders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-employment of faculties (overlooking facts knowable by reasoning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Error arising from not employing reasoning faculties to infer or investigate circumstances that are not immediately sensed but would alter conclusions if attended to.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply reasoning to identify hidden or indirect factors whose recognition would change the conclusion. Example: economic fallacies where visible immediate effects (A's spending) are observed while diffuse, indirect effects (B's investment) are overlooked. Consider indirect, delayed, and systemic consequences, not just immediate appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mal-observation: mistaking inference for perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The error of regarding as direct perception what is in fact inference; confusing what was actually perceived with the inferences drawn from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish clearly between raw sensory perception (what was actually seen/heard) and inferences or interpretations built upon it. Train to report perceptions separately from conclusions. Examples: witnesses mixing inference into testimony; the popular 'seeing' of sunrise/set taken as proof of geocentrism. Cross-examination and analytic habits help separate perception from inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seeing a part for the whole (overlooking diffuse/contrary effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observing only the immediate, concentrated, and obvious effects of a cause while neglecting widely diffused or deeper effects that may be exactly contrary and change the overall evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating causes, search for both immediate and diffuse effects; weigh the aggregate (including long-run and indirect effects) before concluding. Example: apparent employment created by prodigal spending (A) vs. the capital-employment generated by saving/investment (B); free-trade objections that ignore exported-equivalent flows. Use comprehensive causal accounting rather than superficial observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalid universal inferences and unwarranted extrapolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizations that profess to extend beyond what experience can warrant—e.g., from terrestrial order to remote parts of the universe, or asserting universal negatives (impossibilities) from limited experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the limits of induction: avoid inferring absolute impossibility except where grounded in number/extension or the universal law of causality; do not extrapolate beyond the domain directly supported by observed antecedents. Be cautious when extending local regularities to radically different contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolving radically different phenomena into one element
rubrics_metrics.description: The fallacy of attempting to reduce qualitatively different phenomena (differences of kind, not merely degree) into a single element or law (e.g., reducing sensation or color to motion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between showing that one class of phenomena is a condition or cause of another and claiming that the latter is nothing but the former. Even if physical processes are necessary conditions for sensations, that does not explain the qualitative peculiarities (the 'law of color'). Avoid conflating conditions with full explanations of qualitatively distinct phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction by simple enumeration (enumeratio simplex)
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalization by mere enumeration of observed instances without the eliminations and exclusions necessary for secure induction—'This, that, and the other A are B; I cannot think of any A not B; therefore every A is B.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject bare enumeration as proof. Employ the inductive method of separating nature by proper rejections and exclusions, and seek negative instances decisive of the contrary. Bacon's admonition: induction useful for science must use eliminations and exclusions and not rely on the few available instances alone. Avoid social maxims and sweeping claims founded only on readily-available examples.
